# The t-test

::: {.callout-note}
## Video
Coming soon.
:::

::: {.chapter-intro}
**In this chapter:** compare the means of two groups and read the output.
:::

A t-test asks whether the difference between two group means is larger than you would expect by chance. It is one of the most common tests in biology.

```{r}
morph <- read.csv("data/morphometry.csv")
morph$Height <- morph$Height / 10
```

## Question and plot

Do males and females differ in height? Always plot first. The plot shows you roughly how big the difference is, and lets you spot odd values, before any test does.

```{r}
boxplot(Height ~ Sex, data = morph, ylab = "Height (cm)")
```

## Run the test

The formula `Height ~ Sex` is the same as in the boxplot. Read it as "height, split by sex".

```{r}
t.test(Height ~ Sex, data = morph)
```

R runs a **Welch t-test** by default. It does not assume that the two groups have the same spread, so it is a safe choice.

## Read the output

Read the output from the bottom up. Start with the size of the difference, not the p-value.

- **Sample estimates** (bottom lines): the mean height is 159.9 cm for females and 175.0 cm for males, so males are about 15.1 cm taller.
- **95 percent confidence interval:** -16.7 to -13.4. R gives the difference as female minus male, hence the minus signs. A plausible range for the true difference is 13.4 to 16.7 cm.
- **t, df and p-value** (top line): `t` is the difference measured against the variation in the data, and `df` (degrees of freedom) reflects the sample size. The p-value is the probability of seeing a difference at least this large if the true means were equal. That assumption of no difference is called the **null hypothesis**. R prints `p-value < 2.2e-16`, which is R's way of saying "extremely small". Report it as p < 0.001.

Confidence interval, standard error, p-value and the other terms here are explained in the [Glossary](glossary.qmd#from-sample-to-population).

Write it up with the estimate first:

> Males were on average 15.1 cm taller than females (95% CI 13.4 to 16.7 cm; Welch t-test, t = 18.2, d.f. = 152.8, p < 0.001).

## Functions in this chapter

- `boxplot(y ~ group)`: plot a numeric variable by group.
- `t.test(y ~ group)`: compare the means of two groups.

## Your turn

Using `cholesterol.csv`, test whether cholesterol differs between the control and drug groups. Plot it first. How big is the difference, what is its confidence interval, and what would you conclude?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Model answer

```r
chol <- read.csv("data/cholesterol.csv")
boxplot(Cholesterol ~ Treatment, data = chol, ylab = "Cholesterol")
t.test(Cholesterol ~ Treatment, data = chol)
```

Mean cholesterol was 205.7 in the control group and 185.5 in the drug group, a difference of 20.2. The 95% confidence interval is -1.8 to 42.2, which includes zero (p = 0.068).

The drug may lower cholesterol by about 20, but with only six people per group the data are also consistent with no effect, or even a small increase. A larger study is needed.
:::
